query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy (HEA) multilayer protective coatings, resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is governed primarily by the density and chemical complexity of heterophase interfaces, which generate strong solute–dislocation drag and reduce vacancy/dislocation mobility across layer boundaries. These interface-mediated effects raise the effective activation energy and stress exponent for creep and suppress dislocation climb/transmission, thereby lowering the steady-state creep rate compared to coatings with compositionally simpler interfaces or single-layer films of similar hardness and grain size.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited nanocrystalline metallic coating set prepared by physical vapor deposition with matched hardness and layer thickness (10–30 nm): (i) a single-layer HEA film and/or a compositionally simpler binary/ternary multilayer; grain size comparable across samples; minimal residual stress; texture controlled to be similar.
generation.intervention: Laminate the HEA into a multilayer architecture using dissimilar HEA layers to maximize interface chemical disorder and short-range order mismatch, while increasing interface density by reducing layer period to 5–20 nm. Maintain total thickness, hardness, grain size, and texture approximately constant across the set.
generation.conditions: Constant-load indentation creep or micropillar compression creep at temperatures corresponding to ~0.3–0.5 of the average melting temperature of the constituent elements; stresses within the elastic-plastic transition of the films; inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; tests spanning multiple stresses and temperatures for activation energy determination.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrahigh density of compositionally complex heterophase interfaces exhibiting short-range order, local coherency strains, and segregation complexions that impede dislocation transmission/climb and retard vacancy/interstitial diffusion across interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Interfaces with high chemical disorder and short-range order create strong solute–dislocation drag and back-stress, increasing lattice friction near interfaces. The same chemical complexity reduces vacancy mobility and cross-interface diffusion (including along and across interfaces), suppressing dislocation climb-assisted creep. Together, these effects increase the apparent activation energy (Q) and stress exponent (n) for creep and reduce the steady-state creep rate under matched conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline single-layer HEA and/or compositionally simpler multilayer of matched hardness, grain size, and layer thickness, the HEA multilayer with higher interface density and chemical complexity will exhibit measurably lower steady-state creep strain rates across the tested stress–temperature window, higher extracted creep activation energies and stress exponents, reduced indentation depth evolution over time, and microstructural signatures of dislocation pile-ups at interfaces with limited cross-interface transmission. Post-mortem TEM will show dislocations arrested or deflected at interfaces, and chemical mapping will reveal interface complexions consistent with segregation/short-range order.
generation.baseline: A single-layer HEA film or a binary/ternary metallic multilayer with matched hardness, grain size, texture, and layer thickness (10–30 nm) but with lower interface chemical complexity (fewer principal elements and minimal segregation/short-range order).
generation.boundary: The effect is expected when interfaces remain chemically and structurally stable (no gross interdiffusion or amorphization) and layer periods are within ~5–50 nm such that interfaces are the dominant obstacles. At temperatures where interdiffusion erases chemical complexity or where very thin layers (<3–5 nm) lose structural integrity, the advantage may diminish. Strong texture enabling easy slip along interfaces, severe residual stresses causing delamination, or recrystallization that coarsens grains may also negate the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the creep-rate reduction, and the precise increases in Q and n, cannot be predicted here without composition-specific data. The relative contributions of solute–dislocation drag versus vacancy transport retardation may vary with alloy chemistry and interface structure. If grain size, texture, or residual stress are imperfectly matched across samples, they may confound observations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare at least three coatings with controlled variations: (A) single-layer HEA; (B) compositionally simpler multilayer (binary/ternary layers) with matched layer thickness; (C) HEA–HEA multilayer with maximized interface chemical complexity and identical layer thickness to B. Match hardness, grain size, total thickness, and texture across A–C. Perform constant-load indentation creep and micropillar compression creep at multiple temperatures (spanning ~0.3–0.5 Tm) and stresses. Conduct TEM/EDS/EELS or atom probe to assess dislocation–interface interactions and interface complexions pre- and post-creep.
measurements: Steady-state creep strain rate versus applied stress for each sample at each temperature
Activation energy for creep (Arrhenius analysis of strain rate versus temperature at fixed stress)
Stress exponent n from log(strain rate)–log(stress) slopes
Time-dependent indentation depth under constant load
TEM characterization of dislocation configurations near interfaces (pile-ups, transmission events)
Chemical mapping of interfaces for segregation and short-range order indicators
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If sample C (HEA multilayer with high interface chemical complexity) does not exhibit lower steady-state creep rates than A or B across the tested stress–temperature range, and does not show higher extracted activation energies or stress exponents within experimental uncertainty, and TEM does not reveal enhanced dislocation blocking/pile-ups at interfaces relative to B, the hypothesis is falsified.
